input.command: cat -n src/jira.ts; ls; ls src; grep -rn "searchAssigned" --include=*.ts . | grep -v node_modules

input.reason: In src/jira.ts:9, searchAssigned builds the JQL string with `assignee = "${email}"` and does not escape `"` or `\`. The encodeURIComponent call on line 10 only makes the query safe to put in a URL. It does not stop JQL injection. The only caller is the assignedIssues route in src/routes.ts:56, which passes req.body.email straight through. Nothing in the repo checks it first: no email format check, no type check, no escaping. A caller who controls the request body can therefore close the quoted string and add their own JQL clauses. The finding is correct at the only location it lists.
input.failure_scenario: A client sends a body of {"email": "x\" OR project is not EMPTY OR assignee = \"y"} to the assignedIssues route. The JQL becomes `assignee = "x" OR project is not EMPTY OR assignee = "y" ORDER BY created DESC`. Instead of that user's assigned issues, it returns every issue the Jira account can see. An email containing a literal `"` or `\` also breaks the query and makes the search fail.
input.severity_reason: Injection lets a caller widen the search past their own assigned issues, which could expose data. The impact has limits, though. The fetch sends no credentials of its own, so Jira's permissions for that account still apply. Also, the issue route (src/routes.ts:48) already returns any issue by key. It is a real injection flaw, but not full data compromise.
